procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.06.2018 of the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur in CRA No.200 of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur issued a Judgment and Order on 26.06.2018 in CRA No. 200 of 2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via a Special Leave Petition. On 30.11.2018, the Supreme Court issued a limited notice regarding the conviction under section 364-A of the Penal Code, while confirming the conviction under sections 307 read with 120B along with sections 392 read with 397 of IPC. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals.

decision.conviction_status: Conviction under Section 307 IPC read with 120(B) and Section 392 IPC read with 397 is upheld. Conviction under Section 364-A IPC is set aside.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence of life imprisonment for the offence under Section 364-A IPC is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellants for the offence under Section 364-A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 was justified.

facts: The appellants were convicted by the Trial Court and the High Court for offences including Section 364-A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and were sentenced to life imprisonment for it.
The prosecution's evidence to establish the charge under Section 364-A was a phone call made to the victim's father.
The Court found that the prosecution had successfully established the facts of abduction and attempt to murder.
law: To make out a case under Section 364-A IPC, the act of kidnapping or abduction must be coupled with other specific conditions.
Section 364 IPC pertains to the offence of abduction in order to murder.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and found that there was "no worthwhile evidence" presented by the prosecution to satisfy the necessary conditions for a conviction under Section 364-A.
The Court concluded that both the Trial Court and the High Court were "completely misdirected" in holding that the case fell under Section 364-A.
However, the Court determined that the evidence did prove that the victim was abducted with the intent to be murdered, which constitutes an offence under Section 364 IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction under Section 364-A, finding it was not justified due to a lack of evidence. It set aside the conviction and the life sentence for that charge. The Court then converted the conviction to the lesser offence of Section 364 IPC (abduction in order to murder) and sentenced the appellants to ten years of rigorous imprisonment for this specific count, while affirming the convictions for other offences.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 307 read with 120(B) and Section 392 read with 397 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 was justified.

facts: The appellants were convicted by the Trial Court for offences under Sections 307/120B (attempt to murder with criminal conspiracy) and 392/397 (robbery with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The High Court upheld these convictions in a criminal appeal.
law: Section 307 of the IPC pertains to the offence of attempt to murder.
Section 120B of the IPC pertains to the punishment for criminal conspiracy.
Section 392 of the IPC pertains to the punishment for robbery.
Section 397 of the IPC pertains to robbery or dacoity with an attempt to cause death or grievous hurt.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the case and the evidence presented.
While the Court found that the conviction under Section 364-A (kidnapping for ransom) was not justified and modified it, it considered the convictions under the other sections separately.
The Court explicitly stated that it did not find any valid reason to interfere with the convictions under Sections 307/120B and 392/397.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants for the offences under Section 307 read with Section 120B and Section 392 read with Section 397 of the IPC, finding no grounds to warrant interference with the lower courts' decisions on these specific charges.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellants for the offence under Section 364-A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 was justified.
appellant_arguments: There was no evidence to convict the appellants under Section 364-A, and the Trial Court and High Court were completely misdirected in their findings on this charge.
respondent_arguments: The evidence presented by the prosecution, which led to convictions in the Trial Court and the High Court, was sufficient to justify the charge under Section 364-A.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 307 read with 120(B) and Section 392 read with 397 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 was justified.
appellant_arguments: The appellants pleaded not guilty and challenged the conviction, arguing that the prosecution's evidence was insufficient or unreliable, as demonstrated by the cross-examination of witnesses.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution's case was supported by strong witness testimony that withstood lengthy cross-examination without any doubts being cast on the statements, thereby proving the charges.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An offence constitutes an act under Section 364 of the Indian Penal Code when the facts do not justify a conviction under Section 364-A.
obiter: When the evidence of an injured eye-witness is to be appreciated, the legal principles enunciated by the Courts are required to be kept in mind.

A statement is relevant when it gives the opinion of a person as to the existence of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest, of which he would have been likely to be aware, and when such statement was made before any controversy had arisen.
A statement is relevant when it was made by a number of persons, and expressed feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that while the convictions for attempted murder and robbery were justified based on the high evidentiary value of the injured eyewitness's testimony, the conviction under Section 364-A IPC was not. There was a complete lack of evidence to support the specific elements of Section 364-A, and the lower courts were misdirected in their findings. The evidence did, however, prove the offence of abduction in order to murder, justifying a conversion of the conviction to the lesser offence under Section 364 IPC.
legal_tests_applied: When appreciating the evidence of an injured eye-witness, the following legal principles apply: (a) it must be believed that an injured witness would not allow the real culprits to escape and falsely implicate the accused, unless otherwise established, and (b) the evidence of an injured witness has greater evidentiary value and their statements are not to be discarded lightly unless compelling reasons exist.

To convict under Section 364-A IPC, there must be evidence of a threat to cause death or hurt, or conduct giving rise to a reasonable apprehension that such person may be put to death or hurt, in the context of kidnapping for ransom or terrorism.
why_appellant_lost: The court found no good ground to interfere with the convictions under Section 307 IPC (attempted murder) and Section 392 read with 397 IPC (robbery), implicitly accepting the credibility and high evidentiary value of the injured eyewitness testimony as per established legal principles.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution's case for conviction under Section 307 and Section 392/397 was successful because the court applied the legal principle that the evidence of an injured witness has greater evidentiary value and should not be discarded lightly, thereby upholding the findings of the lower courts on these charges.
policy_considerations: The court considered the legislative history and intent behind Section 364-A IPC, noting that it was specifically enacted to address the increasing incidence of kidnapping and abduction for ransom and was later amended to combat the spectre of terrorism. This context informed the court's assessment that the facts of the present case did not align with the specific type of crime the statute was designed to punish.
